e-84.knowledge_point: Determining Vertical Asymptotes of a Rational Function
e-84.worked_solution:
Let's simplify the expression by factoring the denominator. We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-16} \\  & =\frac{1}{({x}^{2}-{4}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{(x+4)(x-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator. So, we find the vertical asymptotes by setting the denominator equal to zero:

$$
(x+4)(x-4) = 0\qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad x=\pm 4.
$$

Consequently, both $x=4$ and $x=-4$ are vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x).$

e-85.knowledge_point: Determining Vertical Asymptotes of Rational Functions by Factoring the Numerator and Denominator
e-85.worked_solution:
We start by factoring the function as much as possible and canceling the common factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}+x-6}{{x}^{2}-5x+6} & =\frac{(x-2)(x+3)}{(x-2)(x-3)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x-2)}(x+3)}{\cancel{(x-2)}(x-3)} \\  & =\frac{x+3}{x-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
x-3 = 0\qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad x=3.
$$

So the *only* vertical asymptote is at $x=3.$

e-86.knowledge_point: Identifying When a Rational Function has no Vertical Asymptotes
e-86.worked_solution:
Let's simplify the expression by factoring both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}+x}{2x+2} & =\frac{x(x+1)}{2(x+1)} \\  & =\frac{x\cancel{(x+1)}}{2\cancel{(x+1)}} \\  & =\frac{x}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the denominator is never zero, we conclude that this function has no vertical asymptotes. A plot of the function is below. Note that it is not defined at $x=-1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13979852/assets/eda5457edafe14fb51fcc75ca75677b199bfc3e0aef8940c66f8aa78cf8cd5c3.png)

e-87.knowledge_point: Determining the Vertical Asymptotes for the Sum of Two Rational Functions
e-87.worked_solution:
First, let's put the two terms over a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x+1} & =\frac{(x+1)}{x(x+1)}+\frac{x}{x(x+1)} \\  & =\frac{x+1+x}{x(x+1)} \\  & =\frac{2x+1}{x(x+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we proceed to set the denominator equal to zero and get

$$
x(x+1) = 0\qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad x=0,-1.
$$

Therefore, the vertical asymptotes are at $x=0$ and $x=-1.$

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
We start by factoring the function as much as possible and canceling the common factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x-6}{{x}^{2}-7x+12} & =\frac{2x-6}{{x}^{2}-4x-3x+12} \\  & =\frac{2(x-3)}{x(x-4)-3(x-4)} \\  & =\frac{2(x-3)}{(x-4)(x-3)} \\  & =\frac{2\cancel{(x-3)}}{(x-4)\cancel{(x-3)}} \\  & =\frac{2}{x-4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
x-4=0\,⟹\,x=4.
$$

So the *only* vertical asymptote is at $x=4.$
